passage:
"Are you awake?" Rukmini whispered from the other bed.
"Yes." Kamal pulled the blanket up. "I keep seeing it. Me, on the stage, forgetting the whole poem. Everyone staring."
"That was Thursday."
"I know. It plays every night. Why does my brain do this?"
"Tell me exactly what happened."
"I forgot line four. I just stood there. Then Mr. Sane prompted me and I finished."
"You finished," said Rukmini. "So what would you do differently?"
"Learn the poem in chunks. And not look at the front row."
"There. That's data, not a verdict. Want to practise tomorrow?"
Kamal laughed softly. "Okay."

qa.q: How does Kamal feel about the memory of the poem at night?
qa.a: Kamal feels ashamed and embarrassed, replaying every night the moment of forgetting the poem on stage while everyone stared.

qa.q: How can Kamal treat the memory as data instead of a verdict?
qa.a: Kamal can work out what went wrong, such as learning the poem in chunks and not looking at the front row, and practise, instead of using it to judge Kamal's worth.

qa.q: How does Rukmini see the moment on stage?
qa.a: Rukmini sees a slip that Kamal recovered from, since Kamal finished the poem after a prompt, and worth learning from rather than agonising over.

grounding: Kamal replays a public failure at night and cringes; talking to Rukmini shrinks it and turns it into data for practice.

passage: Arnab, you think your Tanuja Mashi never made a fool of herself? Listen. I was fifteen, at the district debate in Asansol, and I got up and argued the exact opposite of my team's side. For two full minutes I made the other team's case. The judges were smiling, and my own teammates had their heads in their hands. For weeks I replayed it every night in bed, cringing so hard I'd pull the pillow over my face. Then my friend Shampa caught me brooding on the school steps and said, 'Tell me the whole thing.' So I did, and somewhere in the telling we both started laughing. It felt smaller. Then she asked, 'So what does it teach you?' Read the motion twice. Write your side on your hand. That's all it was: information. I won that same debate the next year. The pillow I kept, Arnab, for sleeping.

qa.q: What mistake did Tanuja make at the district debate?
qa.a: She argued the other team's side for two full minutes.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when replaying it at night?
qa.a: She felt deep shame and embarrassment, cringing so hard she pulled the pillow over her face.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Tanuja's story?
qa.a: Telling Shampa the whole thing, laughing, and then treating it as lessons: read the motion twice, write your side on your hand.

qa.q: How did Shampa see Tanuja's mistake?
qa.a: As something to talk through and learn from, not a verdict on Tanuja.

grounding: An elder's story of replaying a public failure at night, sharing it with a friend and treating it as data rather than a verdict.

passage: Kunal had one job: present the group's science project at the district exhibition. Then the projector died, the laptop charger was missing, and the judges were already standing at their table. He tried to explain from memory, got the numbers muddled, and said 'photosynthesis' when he meant 'respiration'. One judge smiled politely. Someone behind giggled. That night, in the small room he shared with his brother, Kunal lay awake replaying it: the giggle, the smile, his own voice cracking. Every replay made his face burn hotter. By two in the morning he had decided he was just bad at speaking. Next morning, still cringing, he told Vaibhav everything on the walk to school. Vaibhav listened, then said, 'So you learned two things: carry a printout, and practise without slides.' Kunal stopped walking. That was it. Not a verdict on him. Just two things to fix.

qa.q: What word did Kunal say when he meant 'respiration'?
What was Kunal feeling as he replayed the presentation at night?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and cringed harder with every replay, his face burning hotter.

qa.q: How did talking to Vaibhav change the memory?
qa.a: Vaibhav turned it into two lessons, carry a printout and practise without slides, so it became data, not a verdict 🙂

qa.q: How might the judge who smiled politely have seen the moment?
qa.a: The judge may have seen an ordinary nervous student with bad projector luck, not a failure.

grounding: Shows a teen replaying a public stumble at night, telling a friend and treating the memory as lessons rather than a verdict.
